doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: What made Gil Evans unique: textures, electronics, hiring for spirit not blend
summary: Levin describes Gil's textures, openness to electronics, and influence on arrangers.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I should go back to just get your opinion on what made Gil Evans so unique as a musician and person.

Oh that could take a whole other interview here. Well as an orchestrator his ideas, just the sounds and the textures that he envisioned were I think unique at the time when he first started doing it. And they made the sound of some bands that he was writing for, like Claude Thornhill and so forth, and when he applied that to specific projects, like some of his own ten, twelve piece groups, and then of course all the great stuff he did for Miles Davis, I mean just those sounds, the way he used instruments, the way he combined instruments, the voicings that he did were unique. I mean he had such a distinct style. But also that he really created textures. He wasn’t just writing for — he never had a conventional big band. It was a sax section and he got three, four trumpets, some trombones, you’ve got a rhythm section, maybe add tuba, that was a big deal. He never wrote that way. And especially, he got into the 70s, he was — that was why he let me get away with all that stuff of bringing synthesizers into the Village Vanguard, where people were coming in hoping to hear “Sketches of Spain,” and not getting it. But he was open to all that stuff. He thought the electronic sounds were fascinating. And he was into combining synthesizers beeps and barps with flutes and muted trumpets and French horns and tuba and an electric rhythm section. He was open to all those ideas and he heard them and he wrote for them very effectively. He had such a tremendous impact on anybody in jazz who writes music, just sketches arrangements, anybody who goes through that process of telling the guys what to play, what notes to play. Even if it wasn’t a direct contact like I had, I was so fortunate to have for so many years. Everybody is influenced by that to some degree. That’s one major influence or thing about Gil. Another thing that’s always seemed very important to me is Gil was — the way Gil put ensembles together, whether in the studio or for his own live bands — they were based on, he just hired people that he liked. He liked the way they play and he would put them together in an ensemble, really without a whole lot of thought as to whether they would play particularly well together, that is whether the instruments would blend together. Because he was looking, first of all the textures, of getting the notes played, but also there was a spirit in the playing or an input from the players that he wanted to get, that was very meaningful to him. It’s an individual player identity thing that — usually somebody is putting together a big band doesn’t want that. I mean they want five saxes who really blend well together and are playing with the same head. It’s just crossed my mind just a few days ago I went, there was a memorial service at St. Peter’s in New York for Manny Albam. And the Village Vanguard Jazz Band, the Monday night band played there. And these guys have been playing together, this is the one that is the grandchild now of the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band, and it’s a lot of the same guys and the band is just so good.
